strengths: The composite-priority construction is simple and well motivated. The tier-size and ancestor-count arguments provide a convincing route to the static BST depth bound, subject to the usual additive-one correction, and remove the restrictive distribution assumptions of the comparison with Lin et al.

The counterexamples in Section 2.4 provide useful insight into why frequency-only priorities and a single logarithmic transformation can perform poorly. This helps explain the design beyond merely presenting a successful formula.

The cross-entropy interpretation gives an interpretable prediction-dependent upper bound. The working-set score also offers a promising way to encode temporal locality through bounded-total-weight scores that change only at the accessed key.
weaknesses: The update guarantee in Corollary 2.7 is false as stated. Let n = 2^(2^k), initially assign every key weight 1/n, and increase one key's weight to (1+epsilon)/n. Its tier changes from k to k-1, making it the root regardless of the random offsets. Moving it from its original random-treap position requires Theta(log n) expected rotations, while the claimed bound O(|log(w'/w)|) approaches zero with epsilon. The analogous B-tree update bound is also unsupported: Appendix C's delete-and-reinsert argument yields a sum of access bounds, not their logarithmic difference. Appendix D relies on this update guarantee, leaving central dynamic conclusions unproved.

The B-tree high-probability analysis has additional gaps. Theorem C.2 invokes B = O(C_t^(1/2)) for tier populations C_t without establishing this condition; the global restriction on B relative to n does not imply it for individual tiers. The proof also omits negative tiers, which require separate treatment when B grows. Valid handling of small tiers and probability bounds across operations is needed before accepting the external-memory guarantees.

The norm-distance robustness claims in Corollaries C.6–C.9 are not justified and can fail for the stated construction. C.6 incorrectly infers a lower bound on the predicted probability from a lower bound on the true probability. More concretely, take uniform true probabilities and predictions q_i proportional to B^(-2^i), ordered by key. These produce strictly ordered tiers and a chain under the construction that keeps different tiers in separate B-tree nodes. Yet C.6 with epsilon = 1 promises O(m log_B n) cost. Prediction smoothing or a fallback mechanism, followed by revised proofs, is necessary.

Several claims confuse an upper bound with an actual cost comparison. Theorem 2.13 establishes O(m(H(p) + D_KL(p,q))); it does not establish that the additional cost is exactly m times KL divergence or must grow linearly, as asserted in Sections 1.1 and 5.3. Predictions can change within tiers without changing the tree. Similarly, Theorem D.2 substitutes an upper bound on the ideal-score cost for the actual cost when deriving its additive-error comparison. The results should be stated against explicit analytical benchmarks unless stronger stability arguments are supplied.

The experiments contain unexplained inconsistencies that undermine the claimed advantage. Under the stated perfect uniform oracle, every deterministic priority term is identical, so learn-bst and random-treap have the same distribution over trees; the large separation in Figure 4 therefore requires an implementation or protocol explanation. Figure 5 also shows substantial changes in prediction-independent baselines as KL divergence changes, without explaining whether the true workload changes. Section 5.1 fixes n and varies m but describes the horizontal axis as the number of unique items. These issues require a clarified protocol and verified comparisons.

The empirical scope does not substantiate the broader practical claims: experiments cover synthetic static BST workloads, with no evaluation of the proposed B-tree I/O costs, dynamic maintenance, or working-set adaptation. The manuscript also lacks sufficient implementation and workload-generation detail to resolve the anomalies above, including whether oracle frequencies are population or realized frequencies, how comparisons are counted, and what the error bars represent. These limitations are especially consequential because the dynamic and external-memory analyses have unresolved gaps.

The contribution needs clearer positioning against classical weighted randomized search trees. Independent exponential priorities with rates proportional to weights already yield O(1 + log(W/w_x)) expected depth and consequently a cross-entropy bound when predicted probabilities supply the weights. Comparing primarily against frequency-ordered treaps does not establish the novelty or advantage of the static guarantee. The rounded construction and proposed extensions may still contribute, but their benefits over this direct alternative need to be articulated and supported.
